maya.blurb: Conversational and kind. Draws out your story with gentle follow-ups. No tricks.
maya.style: Calm pace · open questions · listens back · encouraging · never combative
maya.company: Talent partner at a fast-growing company

june.blurb: Cares about the mission. Wants to know why this company and why now.
june.style: Friendly and quick · asks about motivation first · tests how sincere the answer is
june.company: Founder and CEO of an early-stage company

nova.blurb: Curious and fast. Moves across the whole field and asks what else is out there.
nova.style: Wide-ranging · compares alternatives · aware of trends · moves sideways rather than deeper
nova.company: Principal at a global consulting firm

priya.blurb: Asks about real past situations until your answer has a clear action and a clear result.
priya.style: Story-based · situation, action, result · patient follow-ups · conflict and failure · separates what you did from what the team did
priya.company: People lead at a large consumer brand

rex.blurb: Hands you a problem you have not seen and watches how you break it down.
rex.style: Open problems · estimates and hypotheticals · reason out loud · changes one constraint mid-answer

diaz.blurb: Calm manager who has done the job. Keeps asking what you specifically did.
diaz.style: Even-tempered · practice over theory · one real example, step by step

atlas.blurb: Senior generalist. Maps what you know and asks about the parts you skip.
atlas.style: Breadth first · across areas · finds the gaps by moving to the next area
atlas.company: Distinguished engineer at a large tech company

bishop.blurb: Wants the failure, the disagreement you lost, and proof you owned it.
bishop.style: Ownership · asks for failure and conflict · distrusts rehearsed answers · what did you do
bishop.company: Hiring director at a fast-growing company

okonkwo.blurb: Rigorous, and keeps changing the problem. Cares how you think under pressure.
okonkwo.style: First principles · structured breakdown · tightening constraints · questions your assumptions
okonkwo.company: Partner at a top strategy firm

kai.blurb: Digs three levels down. Wants the exact decision and the case where it broke.
kai.style: Technical depth · quiet pauses · walk me through exactly what happened
kai.company: Senior staff engineer on a large infrastructure team

voss.blurb: Pushes back on every claim. Wants the number behind the story.
voss.style: Pointed · skeptical · numbers first · how do you know that

lena.blurb: Cares how clearly you land the point. Will ask you to explain the hard thing simply.
lena.style: Audience first · explain it to someone new · rewards a clean opening line · catches rambling
lena.company: Communications lead who has coached hundreds of executives

mirae.blurb: Changes topic every two minutes and keeps the clock running.
mirae.style: Fast topic changes · timed answers · high tempo · rewards adapting quickly
mirae.company: Final-round panel chair at a large tech company

osei.blurb: Looks at how you treat people when it is hard. Asks about putting the team first.
osei.style: Values in action · collaboration stories · how did the team feel · warm but probing
osei.company: Head of people at a values-driven company

devi.blurb: Hands you an open problem and works it with you. Cares how you frame it.
devi.style: Reasoning together · nudges your framing · thinking matters more than the answer
devi.company: Product strategist who reasons out loud with you

amara.blurb: Moves across markets and fields, looking for range and the links you can draw.
amara.style: Across industries · maps the market · who else does this well · connects ideas

sterling.blurb: Senior, exacting, unhurried. Wants the short version first, then the proof.
sterling.style: Formal · headline first · concise under questioning · tests precision
sterling.company: Board-level operator at a large company

tariq.blurb: Pushes hard and fast, talks over you, turns your answer back on you.
tariq.style: Rapid questions · interrupts and challenges · argues the other side · tests composure

log.aria: A sample gap report. It reads a resume with six years of payments work, reads 1,284 open postings, ranks 41 as a fit, and then names the gaps: Kubernetes appears in twelve of those postings and not on the resume; nine postings ask for team leadership while the resume says helped with; six postings ask for a security clearance, so they are removed. It shows the top job at 87 out of 100, notes three bullets that need a number, and lists the six questions the interviewer is most likely to ask.

problem.title: More applications is not the answer.
problem.sub: AI flooded hiring, and recruiters can tell. In one Business Insider test, a mass-apply bot got a 6% response rate. Sending more of the same resume into the same wall does not change the result. Knowing what each posting asks for, and whether your resume says it, does.

s1.label: people now apply to the average corporate opening

s2.label: more applications reaching recruiters since mass-apply tools took off

s3.label: of job seekers think under a quarter of their applications are ever read by a person

problem.source: Sources: The Interview Guys (242) · Greenhouse via Fortune (+400%) · candidate surveys, 2025–2026 (41%)

how.title: Find. Understand. Fix. Practice.
how.sub: Add your resume once. Everything after that is about one question: what does this posting want that you are not saying?

s1.title: It reads the market
s1.body: Thousands of live postings get read and compared against your resume. Jobs outside what you asked for never reach your list.

s2.title: It names the gap
s2.body: Every job leads with the plain sentence that matters: they ask for Kubernetes twice, and your resume never mentions it. Under it sits the fit score, out of 100, with a line saying what the number is and what it is not.

s3.title: You fix the resume
s3.body: Tailor a copy for one job, with the changes shown side by side. Every number in the draft has to trace back to a line on your resume, or the download is blocked until you fix it.

s4.title: Then you practice the interview
s4.body: A live voice interviewer, briefed on that job post and your resume, asks what that panel is likely to ask. You get a report, a transcript, and a recording.

loop.title: One place, from resume to offer.
loop.sub: The job you found produced the gap. The gap produced the resume edit. The resume edit produced the practice question. Each step feeds the next.

match.title: Jobs ranked by how well you fit
match.body: Every job is read against your actual resume and lands on one of four rungs: great fit, good fit, possible, unlikely. The reason is written in plain words, not keyword counts.

resume.title: A resume you can actually fix
resume.body: Import from LinkedIn or PDF, rewrite weak lines, tailor a copy for one job with the changes shown side by side, and export a PDF that scanners can read.

apply.title: Every application, and what happened to it
apply.body: You apply on the company's site. The job moves to Applied by itself, and the board shows exactly where each one stopped: first call, interviewing, final round, offer, or rejected.

studio.title: An interviewer to practice against
studio.body: A live voice interviewer with 18 field playbooks and 28 formats — phone calls, system design, case interviews — that scores you the way the real panel will.

studio.title_machine: Getting the interview is half of it
studio.sub: 63% of job seekers have already faced an AI interviewer in real hiring (Greenhouse, 2026). Practice against ours as many times as you want, with nobody watching.

f1.title: It talks, and interrupts, like a person
f1.body: Live voice: the interviewer follows up, pushes back, and cuts in, in 9 languages with native voices.

f2.title: 18 field playbooks, not trivia lists
f2.body: Law, finance, healthcare, hardware, AI and more. It asks what people inside that field actually ask, and scores through the same lens.

f3.title: It reads the job before you meet
f3.body: The interviewer reads current postings for your exact role, plus the job post you paste, then builds the questions around your resume.

f4.title: A report that changes your next answer
f4.body: Five plain questions answered about your performance, per-question corrections with a stronger answer, a full transcript, and a recording.

f5.title: Notes while you answer, if you want them
f5.body: Short notes when you ramble, dodge the question, or bury the point. Camera-on adds the pressure of a real video call.

report.quote: "Lead with the number. The 40% cost cut arrived at the end of your answer."

q1.a: RoboApply reads your resume, reads live job postings, and tells you two things about each job: how well your resume lines up with it, and exactly what it asks for that your resume does not say. Then it helps you fix the resume and practice the interview with a live AI interviewer.

q2.q: Does RoboApply apply to jobs for me?
q2.a: No. Nothing is ever sent to an employer under your name. You open the company's site and apply there; the job moves to Applied on your board by itself, and you can undo that in one tap if you changed your mind.

q3.q: What does the score out of 100 mean?
q3.a: It says how well your resume lines up with that job post: the title and level, the skills they ask for, experience in that industry, location and pay and visa, and how your career has moved so far. It is not your chance of getting hired, and it never claims to be.

q4.q: Can I really practice a job interview with an AI?
q4.a: Yes, with a live voice interviewer that talks, follows up, and interrupts like a person. Choose from 28 formats and 18 field playbooks (software, law, finance, healthcare and more), interview in any of 9 languages, and get a report with per-question corrections, a transcript, and a recording.

q5.q: How is this different from tools that mass-apply for you?
q5.a: Those tools send more of the same resume. In one Business Insider test, a mass-apply bot got a 6% response rate. RoboApply does the opposite: fewer jobs, each one read properly, with the missing words named so you can fix them before you apply. And the same product then prepares you for the interview.

q6.a: The core product is free forever, plus one practice interview a month. Starter is $15/month with 10 practice interviews; Growth is $29/month with 28. A credit is a 20-minute session charged by the second and refilled monthly. Pay by card, or Alipay in China.

q7.a: Nine: English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, German, Japanese, Korean, and Simplified and Traditional Chinese. Practice interviews work in all nine today, including the report. The interface is fully translated into English, Japanese, and both Chinese variants, with the rest arriving now.

q8.q: Is my data safe, and can I delete it?
q8.a: Your resume, transcripts, and recordings are yours, and nothing is shared with employers. Deleting your account really deletes it, rather than hiding it.
